title: The Wet Firewood that Burned
paragraphs: “Though she is not an angel, I would say even the angels cannot measure up to her.

Even if one were to search vigorously And select the best among one crore women, Searching into the present and the future, There is nobody quite like this damsel beautiful as the moon On the earth or in the myriad worlds purāṇas speak of ; Definitely we cannot find one of her kind.
You would not deny it I am sure! For you have seen her.”
Sitting on the horse-drawn chariot stationary He asked his confidant dear as life a thousand times.
No boredom writ on the face, The friend acquiescent said,
“Yes, yes!”

At that time she was standing unseen behind the surrounding wall. The hero pretending to be unaware of her presence Described her loveliness from head to toe: “She is the pinnacle of beauty; When she dresses her hair in five modes -- Bundling it up, Letting it flowing, Or decorating it in the curled fashion-- My darting eyes Would ask who this enchanting woman is! Is she the angel from heaven? Is she the one called Ramba or Urvaci? Dear friend, why don’t you say something to please my craving heart? Would your life-span decrease if you do so?”
So saying The excited hero stamped on the plank of the chariot That spurred the scared horses to run along with the chariot And they were about to ram against the lightning-like heroine!
He pulled her away and exclaimed “Oh! Is that you? I didn’t know the richly-hued peahen would be here around! O my goodness, you are spared!” “Dear, hope you are not hurt,” he asked with concern.
Taking not his hands held around her, he said, “I have been yearning for it for a long time.” And bashfulness prevented her from responding, “I too.”
“The Cupid has struck his arrow, now I don’t have any business here.” The dear friend said And he left the place within the bating of the eyelid, in the chariot, But not before winking at the hero
And commenting that the rendezvous was fine; The towering trees, plants and bushes Dropped their flowers in the wind And did a good turn, For they made for a fine floral bed!
Nobody was around, Only a bit of fear remained as companion for him.
Guarded by culture native to womenfolk, That naive full moon of a damsel was feasting upon The external beauty of that man.
He expected her to acquiesce in his desire for sex, As does a camphor, Without patiently waiting for the wet wood to dry out and ready to burn.
Though she gave her consent to the union of hearts She didn’t acquiesce in bodily contact And sit aside she did.

She then gave him an oblique look which drank his life He understood the underlying consent. He thought, “Why not take the fruit and relish it? I am granted the consent Not just for two souls to become one But also for two bodies to unite.” He tended to cross the limits.
When she tried to stop him, He said, “I beseech you! We both are meeting amidst many a hurdle Do realize, dear.”
His hands moved about caressing her. She gestured as if saying, “Leave alone the hurdles, now take away the finger probing my waist.” She moved a little away from him.
He then made a request passionate, “I cannot bear it any more, my young parrot! Don’t let me die.”
His entreaties melting her She threw off her bashfulness And let him close in.
Though she initially consented to his passion’s compulsion, It turned out to be the desire of both for union.

> Caressing the heroine’s limbs: > Contriving feigned excuses for the same; > Getting close to her and embracing her; > Speaking of her reserve as impediment to union; > His express regret at the union delayed; > The union that ensues thereon; > The joy of union realized in haste > And his lofty vow of unbroken intimacy -- > These eight situations of ruling import > Occasion utterance by the hero. > > ..... > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 11)
